Posted February 13, 2003

Analysis by Richard Cowan

There has seldom been so much confusion about the medical cannabis issue.

In DEAland, the blowback from the Rosenthal case continues to cause maximum embarrassment for the DEA. At the very least, it is going to be extremely difficult to bring cases before a federal jury in the Bay Area.
See
Astonishing Editorial In New York Times Attacks Rosenthal Prosecution. Finally Taking The Issue Seriously?

Nonetheless, the DEA is locked into the party line to such a degree that they are losing all credibility. The San Diego City Council recently voted 6 to 3 to allow patients to have a pound of harvested cannabis.

This was done over the vehement objections of the DEA and the very prohibitionist San Diego-Union Tribune, which has a long history of reefer madness.
See

The San Diego Union-Tribune Poisons Its Readers. The Albany Times Union Offers An Antidote.

Nonetheless, the DEA is locked into the party line to such a degree that they are losing all credibility. The San Diego City Council recently voted 6 to 3 to allow patients to have a pound of harvested cannabis.

This was done over the vehement objections of the DEA and the very prohibitionist San Diego-Union Tribune, which has a long history of reefer madness.
See

The DEA's spokesnark at the City Council hearing simply reasserted the party line that there is no such thing as medical marijuana. Consequently, the feds were totally ignored.

Even the federal prosecutors in San Diego seem to be losing their nerve. Medical cannabis activist Steve McWilliams was allowed to plead guilty to growing 25 plants, and the feds then dropped charges for a larger grow that could have given him up to 40 years in prison. Also, prosecutors agreed to allow McWilliams to argue the constitutionality of his case before a federal appeals court, which is very unusual. He will be sentenced in April.

His attorney, David Zugman, said, " This is the best deal I've ever been offered by the government. It would be crazy to reject it. "

Of course, things in Holland are much further along.

The International Association for Cannabis as Medicine reports that A change of the Dutch law on controlled substances (Opium Act) will take effect on 17 March 2003. It includes regulations for applications regarding the cultivation of cannabis for medicinal purposes and guidelines for cultivating cannabis.

Private growers will be licensed to grow medical grade cannabis for sale to the Dutch government, which will provide pharmacies in the course of 2003 with medicinal cannabis, so that patients can obtain this with a doctor's prescription.

They will be simultaneously doing research on its benefits.
See
Office of Medicinal Cannabis statement

This is obviously the humane way to handle the issue, in contrast to the practice in other countries, with the patients left to suffer while the bureaucracy stalls research.

As I reported at the first of the year, one of the two (so far) approved suppliers is Institute of Medical Marijuana, a Rotterdam company founded by America medical cannabis exile James Burton, who also had the first license to grow medical cannabis under the old system, in 1993.
See
2003: Major Developments Scheduled for Year. Things to Look Out For and Things to Look Forward To.

Of course, while the Dutch Health Ministry got its act together, Dutch patients have been able to go to selected coffee shops and buy their medicine at a 50% discount under the Mediwiet (medical weed) Program founded by cannabis pioneer Wernerd Bruining and Nol van Schaik of Haarlem in 1996.

Belgium is finally formalizing its tolerance of personal possession, but they still expect their citizens to cross the Dutch border to buy their cannabis. It is also likely that they will follow the Dutch example on medical use, but until then Belgian patients will have to go to the Mediwiet shops.

Meanwhile, in the UK, GW Pharmaceuticals is still planning on having its whole cannabis spray available by the end of the year. However, GW is having a problem finding a partner among the big pharmaceutical companies. Glaxo just declined to play. The problem is not that GW's spray does not work. It is getting rave reviews from MS patients.

Rather, as I reported last May, the UK's National Institute for Clinical Excellence (NICE) -- which is described as " the health economics watchdog " -- has indicated concerns about the " cost effectiveness " of GW's products.

Although GW's whole cannabis derivatives are working as expected for people with MS and other neuromuscular problems, they are relatively expensive. If NICE compares the cost of these derivatives with either bud or hashish, whether smoked, vaporized, or ingested, NICE may choose to limit the derivatives to hospital settings where doctors might insist on them.
See
UK Update: Committee to Recommend De Facto Decrim Tomorrow. Dutch Experience Still Open. Colin Davies Free On Bail. Government Reluctant to Pay for GW's Expensive Products? Analysis by Richard Cowan

GW insists, The Company is scheduled to submit its regulatory application to the Medicines Control Agency during the first quarter of 2003. Subject to regulatory approval, GW aims to launch its first product in the UK towards the end of 2003.

GW is also planning on entering the Canadian market, probably next year.

And speaking of Canada.

As attorney Alan Young predicted, Canada is appealing the Ontario ruling that gave the government six months to come up with a workable medical cannabis program. He said then that, it's the light at the end of the tunnel ...I can't really see the law maintaining any operation after this year. It's sitting on a really precarious foundation. "
See
Canadian Health Minister Seeks Asylum In DEAland; Says Making Her Think About Medical Cannabis Constitutes Torture. In DC They Don't Allow That Sort of Thing. Thinking, That Is.

Monday, Young said, It's very schizophrenic. They're trying to sustain a litigation strategy to support the law while at the same time a political strategy that brings it into question. They're two contradictory policies. "

This is very similar to what happened in December with the Supreme Court challenge to all the Canadian cannabis laws. The government was saying one thing in Parliament and just the opposite in the Court. Now the Justices are going to be more than a little annoyed with the government.
See
Canadian Supreme Court Punts On Cannabis Cases Until Spring. The Games Governments Play Prove The Need for International Debate on Cannabis Prohibition. Special to MarijuanaNews

It is not clear what Health Canada hopes to accomplish by the appeal. It will go to the same Ontario Court that ruled against them two and a half years ago.
See
Canadian Court Says Lack of Provision for Medical Marijuana Violates Fundamental Rights; Gives Parliament 12 Months to Fix Marijuana Prohibition
-- Or There Will Be No Marijuana Laws in Canada.

And that is not the only challenge. Yesterday, Alberta MS patient Grant Krieger's new trial on a charge of possession of marijuana for the purpose of trafficking was delayed until the April 9 arraignments at Alberta Court of Queen's Bench. They are waiting for the Supreme Court of Canada to decide whether it will hear a Crown appeal of Krieger's acquittal on a charge of cultivation.

In December, the Alberta Court of Appeal upheld the original ruling of two years ago, in which the judge said it was unconstitutional for the federal government to prevent Krieger from being able to obtain marijuana to alleviate pain caused by his MS.

Alberta's treatment of Krieger is truly outrageous.

Speaking of outrageous, on Monday Health Minister Ann McLellan told The Globe and Mail editorial board that plans are under way to use the government-sanctioned marijuana growing in Manitoba for open clinical trials. People exempt to the country's laws would agree to be monitored by researchers running these trials. Unlike the Dutch approach, this will take care of only a small number of the patients. Those who don't get this cannabis will be the real guinea pigs.
See
Health Canada Gives $5.7 Million Contract to Company With No Experience to Grow Mediocre Weed for Medical Marijuana Research

Previously, Health Canada had said that they were going to destroy the Manitoba weed, because it was either too potent, not potent enough or not consistent, or something.

But the Globe and Mail reports that now she says, the government has become confident only recently that the cannabis grown under contract by Prairie Plant Systems is of a quality consistent enough to be used in medical trials.

Translation: someone was finally able to explain it to her, and deserves a Nobel Prize in medicine. If I seem a little dubious about McLellan and Health Canada, consider this bit of irony: On the same day that they appealed the ruling that they have to have a workable medical cannabis program in six months, Health Canada announced, Health Canada is advising Canadians to read the labels of all prescription and over-the-counter medications to avoid accidental overdose of acetaminophen, which can lead to serious liver toxicity, and even death.
See
Lethal Dose Of Cynicism From Makers Of Tylenol Poll On Aspirin Dangers
 Context Of Medical Marijuana Debate

It concludes, Canadians should know that ALL medicines, both prescription and over-the-counter, have risks as well as benefits.

Well, I can think of one that has no real risks, but we couldn't make this up!

Finally, to make matters even more interesting, Steve Tuck, the American medical cannabis refugee now living in Vancouver, has developed a cannabis cream that has remarkable analgesic qualities.

People with arthritis, fybromyalgia, and other conditions are getting immediate and long lasting relief. We have formed a company to develop and market the cream. Until Health Canada gets its act together and comes up with a workable medical cannabis program, it will probably have to be sold in the gray market with other medical cannabis products.

It will be interesting to see the reaction of the no-medicine-is-smoked crowd to this.
See
Repeat After Me: No Medicine Is Smoked! No Medicine Is Smoked! No Medicine Is Smoked! That's It. You Are Now Qualified To Start Your Very Own Government Funded Anti-Drug Group!


They can't very well say that no medicine is rubbed on you. Of course, they have ignored the existence of vaporizers, but this cream is going to present them with a different problem. Or they may welcome it.

After all, in 1998 the DEA rushed the down-scheduling of Marinol when a number of medical marijuana initiatives passed.
See
Two Days After The Medical Marijuana Initiatives
The DEA Proposes Making Marinol A Schedule III Drug!! " Like Codeine With Tylenol. " More Like Cynicism With Desperation

But that really would not help the prohibitionist cause. On the contrary, GW's research has proven that whole cannabis extracts meaning whole cannabis really works, and this cream does the same.

The reason that the DEA has to insist that there is no such thing as medical marijuana is that having millions of people using it under medical supervision will prove that the prohibitionists have been lying to the people for almost a century.

But time is running out for the suppression of medical cannabis. The only question is how many people will have to suffer and die before common sense and common decency triumph.
See
World AIDS Day: More Proof That the Suppression Of Medical Cannabis Indeed Cannabis Prohibition Itself Is Mass Murder. Analysis by Richard Cowan

As usual, the Dutch lead the way, but Canada will not be far behind. We are winning!
